An invertebrate is any animal that does not have a backbone.

That's the heart of it. The backbone — also called the spine or vertebral column — is that column of bones running down the back of animals like humans, dogs, fish, and birds. Invertebrates simply don't have one. No backbone, no internal spine — that's what puts an animal in this category.

Examples you likely already know: a butterfly, an earthworm, a crab, a jellyfish, a snail, a spider, an octopus. None of them have a backbone. All of them are invertebrates.
The Contrast That Makes It Click

To truly understand "invertebrate," it helps to understand what it's being contrasted with.

Animals are broadly divided into two groups:

Vertebrates — animals that do have a backbone. This includes fish, frogs, snakes, birds, and all mammals (including you). They have an internal skeleton made of bones or cartilage, and the backbone is the central column of that skeleton.

Invertebrates — animals that do not have a backbone. This is everything else in the animal kingdom — and "everything else" turns out to be the vast majority of animals on Earth.

In fact, roughly 97% of all animal species on Earth are invertebrates. Vertebrates — despite being the animals we tend to think about most — are actually a small, specialized minority.
But If There's No Backbone, How Do They Hold Together?

This is a smart question, and it reveals something fascinating.

Invertebrates have evolved several different ways to support their bodies without an internal spine:

Exoskeleton — Instead of bones on the inside, some invertebrates have a hard shell or outer casing on the outside. Insects (like beetles and grasshoppers), crabs, lobsters, and shrimp all have this. Think of a crab's hard shell — that's not a house it borrowed; that shell is the crab's skeleton, worn on the outside.

Shell — Snails, clams, and oysters grow a hard mineral shell around their soft bodies. The shell provides protection and structure, though it is separate from the animal's soft tissue.

Hydrostatic skeleton — Worms and jellyfish use the pressure of fluids inside their bodies to maintain shape and allow movement. It's like how a water balloon holds its form — not because of rigid bones, but because of internal pressure.

No rigid structure at all — Some invertebrates, like sea anemones and coral polyps, are soft-bodied and rely on the surrounding water to support them. Out of water, they collapse.

So invertebrates are not simply "animals that lack something." They have developed their own brilliant, diverse solutions to the basic challenges of having a body.

Invertebrates are not one single family of related animals. They are a massive and wildly diverse collection of creatures spread across many distinct groups. Here are the main ones:

Insects — By far the largest group of animals on Earth. Beetles, ants, bees, butterflies, flies, mosquitoes, and dragonflies are all insects. They have six legs, three body segments, and typically an exoskeleton. There are more species of insects than of all other animals combined.

Arachnids — Spiders, scorpions, ticks, and mites. They have eight legs (not six, which is a common way to distinguish them from insects).

Crustaceans — Crabs, lobsters, shrimp, barnacles, and woodlice (the tiny armored bugs you find under rocks). Most live in water, though some like woodlice live on land. They have an exoskeleton and typically two pairs of antennae.

Mollusks — A huge and varied group including snails, slugs, clams, mussels, oysters, squids, and octopuses. Mollusks are known for soft bodies, and many (though not all) have shells. Octopuses are perhaps the most intellectually remarkable invertebrates — they can solve puzzles, use tools, and have surprisingly complex nervous systems.

Worms — This informal grouping includes earthworms, flatworms, and roundworms. Earthworms are especially important — they tunnel through soil, which aerates the ground and allows plant roots to grow.

Echinoderms — Starfish (sea stars), sea urchins, sea cucumbers, and brittle stars. These are exclusively ocean animals. They have a unique five-part body symmetry and tiny tube-like feet they use to move and grip surfaces.

Cnidarians — Jellyfish, corals, sea anemones, and hydras. These are simple, ancient animals with stinging cells they use to capture prey. Coral reefs — some of the richest ecosystems on Earth — are built from the skeletons of tiny cnidarians called coral polyps.

Sponges (Porifera) — The simplest animals alive. Sponges have no brain, no muscles, no nervous system, and no organs. They are essentially living filters — water flows through their porous bodies and they absorb nutrients from it. They are animals, however, despite appearing more like plants.

Myriapods — Centipedes and millipedes. Centipedes are fast-moving predators with one pair of legs per body segment; millipedes are slow, plant-eating animals with two pairs of legs per segment.

Invertebrates range from the almost unimaginably small to the surprisingly large.

At the tiny end, some invertebrates — like certain mites and roundworms — are so small they are invisible to the naked eye.

At the large end, the giant squid is an invertebrate that can reach lengths of up to 13 metres (43 feet), making it one of the largest animals on Earth. The coconut crab, an invertebrate that lives on tropical islands, is the largest land-dwelling arthropod, with a leg span that can reach nearly a metre.

Virtually everywhere. Invertebrates inhabit every environment on the planet — deep oceans, rainforests, deserts, freshwater rivers, polar regions, soil, and the air. Some live as parasites inside other animals. Some live in scalding volcanic vents at the bottom of the ocean. Some thrive in the coldest places on Earth. Their adaptability is one reason they dominate the animal kingdom numerically.

In strict scientific classification, "invertebrate" is what biologists call a paraphyletic group — meaning it does not represent a single family of animals that all descended from one unique common ancestor. Instead, it is a convenient umbrella term for all animals that happen to lack a backbone.

This is different from a group like "mammals," where every member shares a specific common ancestor and a set of defining traits (warm blood, fur, nursing young with milk). Invertebrates are grouped together not because they share something, but because they all lack the same thing.

This does not make the word any less useful or valid — biologists use it constantly, and it remains one of the most important organizing concepts in zoology. It simply means you should understand it as a broad, practical category rather than a tight biological family.

Invertebrates are not just numerous — they are foundational to life on Earth.

Pollination: Bees, butterflies, beetles, and other invertebrates pollinate the majority of flowering plants, including most of the crops humans eat.

Decomposition: Worms, beetles, and many other invertebrates break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil. Without them, ecosystems would collapse under their own waste.

Food chains: Invertebrates are a primary food source for most fish, birds, amphibians, and reptiles. If invertebrates disappeared, the collapse in the food chain would be catastrophic at every level.

Soil health: Earthworms alone transform soil by tunneling through it, improving drainage, aeration, and fertility.

Reef building: Coral polyps — tiny invertebrates — have built the Great Barrier Reef and every other coral reef on Earth over millions of years, creating ecosystems that support roughly 25% of all marine species.

An invertebrate is any animal without a backbone. They are the dominant form of animal life on Earth — representing around 97% of all animal species — and they include everything from butterflies and beetles to crabs, jellyfish, octopuses, earthworms, and coral. Despite lacking a spine, they have evolved remarkable structures like exoskeletons, shells, and fluid-based support systems to build and maintain their bodies. They are astonishingly diverse in size, shape, habitat, and complexity, and they quietly keep the natural world functioning through pollination, decomposition, soil maintenance, and forming the base of most food chains.
